steps.prompt: It's fun. Now how do real players get it?
steps.sub: Two gates stand between your build and players: it must hold 72fps, and it must travel the store path — dev account, signed APK, listing, review. By the end you'll know both, in order.

steps.prompt: Before you even think about the store, what's the hard performance bar a VR game must hold?

options.t: A steady 72fps — drop below and players get motion sick

steps.why: On Quest, the bar is a rock-steady 72fps (~13.9 ms per frame). Below it, the world judders and players feel sick — and Meta will reject a build that performs badly. Menus and enemy counts don't matter if the frame rate isn't there.
hints: It's the same number from the game-loop lesson — the frame budget.
Comfort in VR is non-negotiable; what frame rate keeps players from feeling sick?

steps.prompt: 3 common ways to claw back frame rate.
steps.sub: Tap each card. These are the first knobs you turn to hit 72fps.

cards.b: Each material/mesh the GPU draws separately is a 'draw call'. Combine meshes & share materials so the GPU does fewer, bigger jobs.
4K textures eat memory and bandwidth on a mobile GPU. Drop to 1K/2K — players rarely notice, the headset thanks you.
Fewer triangles per model = less to transform each frame. Use lower-poly meshes or LODs for distant objects.

steps.prompt: Sort each action: does it help PERFORMANCE, or is it part of the SHIP path?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin.

items.t: Combine meshes to cut draw calls
Submit the store listing for review

hints: Performance = making each frame cheaper. Ship = paperwork + packaging to reach players.
Accounts, APKs, listings, and review are all part of getting it OUT the door.

steps.prompt: Your game runs at 72fps. To put it on the Quest store, what's the FIRST thing you need?
steps.sub: You can't upload anything without this.

options.t: A Meta developer account (and an app created in the dashboard)

steps.why: The store path starts with identity: a Meta developer account and an app entry in the dashboard. Only then can you build a signed APK and attach it to that app. Reviews come after the game is live, not before.
hints: Before you can build or upload, the store needs to know WHO you are.
Reviews require the game to already be published. What comes first?

steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the journey from a working build to a live store page.

cards.b: Register as a Meta developer and create the app entry in the dashboard. This is your store identity.
Build a release APK signed with your keystore — Meta only accepts signed builds, and the signature proves it's really yours.
Title, description, screenshots, a trailer, age rating, comfort level. This is the page players actually see.
Meta tests your build for performance, comfort, and policy. Pass → it goes live; fail → fix the notes and resubmit.

steps.prompt: Tap the ship steps in the order you'd actually do them.
steps.sub: From a finished, fast-enough build to a game players can download.
chips: Create a Meta developer account + app entry
Fill in the store listing (screenshots, description)
Build and upload a signed APK
hints: You need the identity before you can upload a build.
Account → APK → listing → review. Review is always last.

steps.prompt: Walk your finished VR game from your laptop to a live store page.
steps.sub: Pick the right next move at each gate. The release log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Get a 72fps build published on the Quest store.

turns.q: What do you do before anything store-related?
options: Optimize: batch draw calls, shrink textures, cut polys until it holds 72fps
Submit it anyway and hope reviewers don't notice
Add more enemies to make it impressive

turns.q: What kind of build does Meta require?

turns.situation: The build is uploaded and the listing (screenshots, description, comfort rating) is filled in.
options: Submit for review and wait for Meta's pass

hints: Fix performance first, then identity, then build, then listing, then review.
You can't submit for review until there's a signed build AND a filled-in listing.

steps.sub: Tap each, then check all at once.

statements.t: Meta can reject a build purely for poor performance, even if it's fun.
statements.why: Yes — comfort is policy. A build that can't hold frame rate makes players sick, so Meta will fail it in review regardless of how good the gameplay is. Fix performance before you submit.

statements.t: You can upload an unsigned debug APK to the store.
statements.why: No — the store only accepts a SIGNED release APK. The signature ties the build to your keystore and proves it's genuinely yours; debug builds are rejected.

statements.t: Submitting for review is the last step, after the listing and the signed build are ready.
statements.why: Right — review is the final gate. Meta needs a complete listing and an uploaded signed build before there's anything to review.

hints: Think about why a juddery game is a comfort (and therefore policy) problem.
What's always the very last action — and what must exist before it?

steps.prompt: Make it yours — plan YOUR ship.
steps.sub: Not graded. This becomes your release checklist for the game you're building.

fields.label: What's the ONE optimization you suspect your game will need first?
fields.ph: e.g. shrink my 4K wall textures, or merge the repeated crates to cut draw calls
